blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Ionic equilibrium is a fundamental concept in chemistry that describes the balance established between ions and molecules in a solution for a weak electrolyte or a reversible reaction. It is governed by the principles of chemical equilibrium and applies to solutions containing acids, bases, or salts.

rows: Substances that completely dissociate into ions in solution.
Substances that partially dissociate into ions in solution.

blocks.title: Ostwald’s Dilution Law
blocks.text: According to Ostwald’s dilution law when solution of a weak electrolyte is diluted then the degree of ionization of weak electrolyte increases, and at infinite dilution it remains 100% dissociated. ($\alpha \propto \sqrt{\text{Dilution}}$ )

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Treating a non-electrolyte as an electrolyte
Electrolytes are substances that dissociate into ions when dissolved in water, allowing the solution to conduct electricity, sugar (sucrose) is a non-electrolyte

Non-electrolytes, on the other hand, do not dissociate into ions in solution and therefore do not conduct electricity, sodium chloride (NaCl) is an electrolyte.

  • Assuming that weak electrolytes produce the same number of ions as strong electrolytes when, in fact, they produce fewer ions despite having the same concentration as compared to strong electrolyte.
  • Assuming ionization or dissociation happens in the same way in all solvents, neglecting the fact that solvents like water are key to the process.
  • Assuming that the degree of ionization (α) is directly proportional to the concentration of the weak electrolyte, but it is inversely proportional to the square root of it's concentration .

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Water in ionic equilibrium revolves around the role of water in acid-base chemistry and dissociation processes, particularly its involvement in the autoionization of water and its effect on the ionization of weak acids and bases. Water is not just a solvent but also participates in the establishment of equilibrium in aqueous solutions, impacting pH, the concentration of ions, and the behavior of acids and bases.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Using an incorrect value for Kw, such as assuming it is always 1×10−14 regardless of temperature, remember, Kw​ is temperature-dependent (At 25∘C, Kw=1×10−14).
  • Neglecting the contributions of H+ and OH− from water itself in extremely dilute solutions of acids or bases, include H+ orOH−  from water autoprotolysis (1×10−7 M at 25∘C) when the acid/base concentration is very low.
  • Believing that neutral solutions always have a pH of 7, At $25^\circ$C, neutral pH is 7, but at other temperatures $pH_{\text{neutral}} = \frac{1}{2} pK_w$.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Salt hydrolysis is defined as the process in which water reacts with a cation or anion or both of salt to change the concentration of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions of water.

Salt hydrolysis refers to the interaction of salt ions with water molecules to form either acidic or basic solutions. This process occurs when salts dissociate into their constituent ions in water, and these ions react with water molecules, potentially affecting the pH of the solution. The nature of the resulting solution (acidic, neutral, or basic) depends on the type of salt and the ions it produces.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Not correctly identifying whether a salt is formed from a strong acid and a strong base, a strong acid and a weak base, a weak acid and a strong base, or a weak acid and a weak base, different types of salts exhibit different behaviors in solution, especially in terms of hydrolysis.
  • Forgetting to account for the concentration of the salt in the solution when calculating the degree of hydrolysis or pH, the degree of hydrolysis depends on both the hydrolysis constant (Kh​) and the concentration of the salt.
  • Not considering the common ion effect in solutions where the salt dissociates into ions that are already present in the solution.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• A buffer solution is a solution that resists changes in its pH when small amounts of an acid or a base are added. It typically consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid. Buffer solutions maintain a relatively constant pH because the weak acid (or base) neutralizes added bases (or acids), and the conjugate base (or acid) helps neutralize added acids (or bases).
  • The pH of buffer solution does not depend on the volume of solution. Hence, solution can be diluted without change in pH.
  • The pH of buffer solution remains constant even if it is kept for a long time.
  • Change in pH of a solution occurs due to change in concentration of free H+ or OH– ions.

blocks.title: Type of Buffer Solution
blocks.text:
Buffer Solution
Introduction
A. Definition: A solution which resists the change in pH and whose pH does not change significantly on addition of small amount of strong acid or strong base is called buffer solution.
B. Properties of buffer solution:
(i) The pH of buffer solution does not change appreciably upon the addition of small amount of either strong acid or strong base.
(ii) The pH of buffer solution does not depend on the volume of solution. Hence, solution can be diluted without change in pH.
(iii) The pH of buffer solution remains constant even if it is kept for a long time.
Change in pH of a solution occurs due to change in concentration of free H+ or OH- ions.

A. Simple buffer solution: -

Aqueous solution of weak acid-weak base (WA - WB) type of salt.
Ex. CH3COONH4, NH4CN, AgCN etc.
pH = 7 + (1/2)pKa - (1/2)pKb                                                  [pH does not depend on concentration]
CH3COO- + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + NH4OH.

B. Mixed Buffer Solution:

(i) Acidic Buffer Solution

  • The solution in which weak acid and its conjugate base are present.
  • Or an aqueous solution of a mixture of weak acid and salt of the same weak acid with any strong base is called an acidic buffer solution.
Example:

  • CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa
Weak Acid (WA) + Weak Acid Salt Base (WASB)
CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺
CH₃COONa → CH₃COO⁻ + Na⁺
[CH₃COOH + CH₃COO⁻] + Na⁺              (Spectator ion)
Buffer Action:

Case 1:

  • Suppose that a small amount of strong acid is added to the buffer solution. The H⁺ ions of the acid react with the basic component, CH₃COO⁻ ions in the buffer.
CH₃COO⁻ (aq) + H⁺ ⇌ CH₃COOH (aq)
Most of the added H⁺ ions are consumed because the concentration of CH₃COO⁻ in the buffer solution is high. The reaction nearly goes to completion because CH₃COOH is a weak acid and its ions have a strong tendency to form non-ionized CH₃COOH molecules. Due to the removal of most of the added H⁺ ions, there is no appreciable decrease in pH.
Case 2:

  • If a small quantity of strong base is added to the buffer solution, the OH⁻ ions are consumed by the acidic component CH₃COOH.
CH₃COOH (aq) + OH⁻ (aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ (aq) + H₂O (ℓ)
The concentration of ions is high in the buffer solution. Hence most of the added OH⁻ ions are consumed. The reaction goes nearly to completion because CH₃COOH is a weak acid and its ions have a strong tendency to form non-ionized CH₃COOH molecules. Thus, there is no appreciable increase in pH.
( a) pH of Acidic Buffer Solution:

CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa
Acid + Salt
CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺
CH₃COONa → CH₃COO⁻ + Na⁺

Kₐ = [CH₃COO⁻][H⁺] / [CH₃COOH]
Or [H⁺] = Kₐ[CH₃COOH] / [CH₃COO⁻]

Taking the negative log of both sides:
pH = pKₐ - log([Acid] / [Conjugate base])
Or
pH = pKₐ + log([Conjugate base] / [Acid])

pH Range of Acidic Buffer Solution:

It depends on the pKₐ of the acid and the ratio of salt to acid concentrations.

[CH₃COOH] : [CH₃COONa]

  • If 1 : 1 → pH = pKₐ
  • If 10 : 1 → pH = pKₐ + 1
  • So pH range: pH = pKₐ ± 1
Maximum Buffer Action Condition of Acidic Buffer Solution:

[CH₃COOH] : [CH₃COONa] = 1 : 1
pH = pKₐ

Basic Buffer Solution:

Definition:
The solution in which weak base and its conjugate acid are present. Or an aqueous solution of a mixture of weak base and salt of the same weak base with any strong acid is called a basic buffer solution.

Example:

  • NH₄OH + NH₄Cl
NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
NH₄Cl → NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻
[NH₄OH + NH₄⁺] + Cl⁻ (Spectator ion)
  • Buffer Action (for Basic Solution):
Case 1:

  • If a small amount of strong acid is added to the buffer solution, the H⁺ ions are consumed by NH₄OH.
NH₄OH (aq) + H⁺ ⇌ NH₄⁺ (aq) + H₂O (ℓ)
Most of the added H⁺ ions are neutralized by NH₄OH and there is no appreciable change in pH.
Case 2:

  • When a small amount of strong base is added to the buffer solution, the OH⁻ ions react with ions to produce non-ionized NH₄OH molecules.
NH₄⁺ (aq) + OH⁻ (aq) ⇌ NH₄OH (aq)
The concentration of ions is high in the buffer solution. Hence most of the added OH⁻ ions are consumed. The reaction goes nearly to completion because NH₄OH is a weak base and its ions have a strong tendency to form non-ionized NH₄OH molecules. Thus, there is no appreciable increase in pH.
pOH of Basic Buffer Solution:

[NH₄OH + NH₄Cl]

  • NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
  • NH₄Cl → NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻
Kᵦ = [NH₄⁺][OH⁻] / [NH₄OH]
Or
[OH⁻] = Kᵦ[NH₄OH] / [NH₄⁺]

Taking the negative log of both sides:
pOH = pKᵦ + log([NH₄⁺] / [NH₄OH])

Henderson's Equation (for Basic Solution):

pOH = pKᵦ + log([Salt] / [Base])
Or
pOH = pKᵦ + log([Conjugate acid] / [Base])

pOH Range of Basic Buffer Solution:

It depends on the pKᵦ of the base and the ratio of salt to base concentrations.

[NH₄OH] : [NH₄Cl]

  • If 1 : 10 → pOH = pKᵦ + 1
  • If 10 : 1 → pOH = pKᵦ - 1
  • So pOH range: pOH = pKᵦ ± 1
Maximum Buffer Action Condition of Basic Buffer Solution:

NH₄OH : NH₄Cl
pOH = pKᵦ

Buffer Capacity:

Definition:

  • It is defined as the number of moles of strong acid (or strong base) added to one liter of a buffer solution to change its pH by one unit.
  • It measures the effectiveness of a buffer.
  • Larger the value of buffer capacity, more resistant is the solution to pH change.
$\text{Buffer Capacity} = \frac{\text{Number of moles of acid or base added per liter}}{\text{Change in pH of buffer solution} }$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Treating strong acids or bases as weak acids or bases in a buffer system, Strong acids (e.g., HCl) and strong bases (e.g., NaOH) dissociate completely in water and do not form a buffer. Only weak acids or bases, which do not dissociate completely, can form effective buffers.
  • Using the wrong pKa or pKb value for the acid or base, always check that the pKa or pKb values used are correct and applicable to the substances in your buffer system.
  • Miscalculating the ratio of the concentrations of acid and base, ensure that the ratio of the base and acid concentrations is correct in the Henderson equation. If the concentrations are mixed in equal amounts, the ratio should be 1, but if they differ, this should be reflected in the equation.
  • Not accounting for volume changes when adding acid/base to the buffer solution, when add a strong acid or base to a buffer, the volume and concentration of the acid/base components may change. You should consider the dilution effect and recalculate the concentrations if necessary.
  • Using the buffer in a pH range outside its effective range, buffers are effective only within a specific pH range, typically within ±1 pH unit of the pKₐ. Make sure the target pH falls within this range for the buffer to be effective.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Calculate volume of 0.1 M HCOONa solution that should be added into 50 ml of 0.05 M of HCOOH solution to make a buffer solution of pH = 4. [Given: $pK_a$= 3.7]

1) 25 ml
2) 50 ml
3) 100 ml
4) 150 ml
blocks.answer:
Given:

pH=4

pKa=3.7

Suppose ‘V’ ml volume of HCOONa solution is added then final concentration would be as following:

$[\text{HCOONa}] = \frac{0.1V}{50 + V}$

$[\text{HCOOH}] = \frac{0.05 \times 50}{50 + V}$

$\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log \left( \frac{[\text{HCOONa}]}{[\text{HCOOH}]} \right)$

$4 = 3.7 + \log \left( \frac{0.1V}{0.05 \times 50} \right)$

$0.3 = \log \left( \frac{V}{25} \right)$

$\log 2 = \log \left( \frac{V}{25} \right) \Rightarrow 2 = \frac{V}{25} \Rightarrow V = 50 \, \text{mL}$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Solubility refers to the maximum amount of a substance (solute) that can dissolve in a solvent to form a homogeneous solution at a given temperature and pressure.
  • The solubility is typically expressed in terms of grams per liter (g/L), moles per liter (mol/L), or other units depending on the substance.
  • The solubility product (denoted as $K_{sp}$) is an equilibrium constant that represents the solubility of an ionic compound in water. It is the product of the concentrations of the ions involved, each raised to the power of their respective coefficients in the dissociation equation.

blocks.title: Solubility Product (Ksp) and Solubility Formula Table:
Common Ion Effect on Solubility
blocks.text: Solubility of substances always decreases in the presence of common ion. According to Le-Chatelier's principle on increasing common ion concentration equilibrium shifts in backward direction until the equilibrium is re-established, so, the solubility of substances decreases but Ksp remains same because it is an equilibrium constant which depends only on temperature.

blocks.title: Condition of Precipitation
blocks.text:
Ionic product (IP) of an electrolyte is defined in the same way as Ksp. The only difference is that ionic product (IP) expression contains the initial concentration of ions or the concentration at any time (Solution is under saturated or over saturated) whereas the expression of Ksp contains only saturated condition (equilibrium) concentration.

• IP < Ksp : The solution is unsaturated, and precipitation will not occur.
    • IP = Ksp : The solution is saturated, and solubility equilibrium exists.
    • IP > Ksp : The solution is supersaturated and hence precipitation of the compound will occur.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Mixing up solubility and solubility product.
  • Applying the concept of Kₛₚ to strong electrolytes like NaCl or KNO₃ while Kₛₚ is only applicable .
  • Assuming that a sparingly soluble salt  dissociates completely in solution when calculating Kₛₚ, some salts, such as AgCl, only partially dissociate in water. Overestimating dissociation can lead to incorrect Kₛₚ values and solubility predictions.
  • Ignoring the effect of common ions in a solution when calculating solubility, the presence of a common ion (an ion already present from another source) will shift the dissolution equilibrium, reducing the solubility of the salt according to Le Chatelier's Principle. This is often ignored in calculations.
  • Using the wrong stoichiometry when writing the Kₛₚ expression.
  • Using Kₛₚ to predict precipitation without calculating the ionic product (Qₛₚ), the precipitation of a salt occurs when the ionic product $Q_{sp}$ exceeds $K_{sp}$. If $Q_{sp}$>$K_{sp}$, precipitation occurs; if $Q_{sp}$ < $K_{sp}$, no precipitation will occur.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
The core concept of acid-base theory in ionic equilibrium revolves around the ability of substances to either donate or accept protons (H⁺ ions) or to contribute hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in an aqueous solution.

  • Arrhenius Concept
  • Bronsted-Lowry Concept
  • Lewis Concept

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
Arrhenius Theory restricting Acid-Base Behavior to Aqueous Solutions:

• Assuming substances are acids or bases only when dissolved in water.

Example: NH₃ is a base, but it doesn’t produce OH⁻ directly in water (it reacts with water to form NH₄⁺).

  • Failing to recognize acid-base behavior in non-aqueous systems.
Example: HCl in benzene doesn’t dissociate into H⁺ and Cl⁻ but still behaves as an acid.

Bronsted-Lowry Theory Ignoring the Role of Solvent:

  • Assuming proton donation or acceptance occurs without considering the medium.
Example: HCl is a strong acid in water but behaves differently in non-aqueous solvents.

  • Overlooking Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
Example: In NH₃+H₂O→NH₄⁺+OH⁻, NH₄⁺ and NH₃ are conjugate acid-base pairs, but students often miss this relationship.

Confusing Lewis and Bronsted-Lowry Definitions:

  • Mistake: Believing a Lewis acid must always donate H⁺ or contain hydrogen.
Example: BF₃ is a Lewis acid even though it has no hydrogen.

  • Restricting Lewis acid-base reactions to proton transfer.
  • Example: AlCl₃+Cl⁻→[AlCl₄]⁻ is a Lewis acid-base reaction where AlCl₃ accepts an electron pair.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Gaseous hydrogen chloride is a very poor conductor of electricity but a solution of hydrogen chloride in water is a good conductor. This is due to the fact that :-

(1) Water is a good conductor of electricity

(2) Hydrogen chloride ionises in water

(3) A gas cannot conduct electricity but a liquid can

(4) HCl does not obey Ohm's law where as the solution does
blocks.answer: (2) Hydrogen chloride ionises in water due to Arrhenius concept.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Water in ionic equilibrium revolves around the role of water in acid-base chemistry and dissociation processes, particularly its involvement in the autoionization of water and its effect on the ionization of weak acids and bases. Water is not just a solvent but also participates in the establishment of equilibrium in aqueous solutions, impacting pH, the concentration of ions, and the behavior of acids and bases.

blocks.title: pH of Mixture of Acid and Base
blocks.text:
pH of Mixture of Acid and Base

$\text{(a) pH of mixture of strong acids:} \\ N_1V_1 + N_2V_2 + N_3V_3 + \ldots = NV \\ V = \text{Volume of final solution} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + \ldots \\ N = \text{Normality of final solution} = [H^+] \text{ in final solution.}  \\ \\ \text{(b) pH of mixture of strong bases:} \\ N_1V_1 + N_2V_2 + N_3V_3 + \ldots = NV \\ V = \text{Volume of final solution} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + \ldots \\ N = \text{Normality of final solution} = [OH^-] \text{ in final solution.} \\ \\ \text{(c) pH of mixture of strong acids and strong bases:} \\ \text{For acid:} \\ N_1V_1 + N_2V_2 + N_3V_3 + \ldots = (NV)_\text{Acid} \\ \text{For base:} \\ N_1V_1 + N_2V_2 + N_3V_3 + \ldots = (NV)_\text{Base} \\  \text{(i) If } (NV)_\text{Acid} > (NV)_\text{Base} \text{ then solution is acidic.} \\ NV = (NV)_\text{Acid} - (NV)_\text{Base} \\ [H^+] = N $

$\text{(ii) If } (NV)_\text{Base} > (NV)_\text{Acid} \text{ then solution is basic.} \\ NV = (NV)_\text{Base} - (NV)_\text{Acid} \\ [OH^-] = (NV)_{Acid}$

$ \text{(iii) If, } (NV)_\text{acid} = (NV)_\text{base} \text{ then solution is neutral.}$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Salt hydrolysis is defined as the process in which water reacts with a cation or anion or both of salt to change the concentration of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions of water.

Salt hydrolysis refers to the interaction of salt ions with water molecules to form either acidic or basic solutions. This process occurs when salts dissociate into their constituent ions in water, and these ions react with water molecules, potentially affecting the pH of the solution. The nature of the resulting solution (acidic, neutral, or basic) depends on the type of salt and the ions it produces.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Solubility refers to the maximum amount of a substance (solute) that can dissolve in a solvent to form a homogeneous solution at a given temperature and pressure.
  • The solubility is typically expressed in terms of grams per liter (g/L), moles per liter (mol/L), or other units depending on the substance.
  • The solubility product (denoted as $K_{sp}$) is an equilibrium constant that represents the solubility of an ionic compound in water. It is the product of the concentrations of the ions involved, each raised to the power of their respective coefficients in the dissociation equation.

blocks.title: Common Ion Effect on Solubility
blocks.text: Solubility of substances always decreases in the presence of common ion. According to Le-Chatelier's principle on increasing common ion concentration equilibrium shifts in backward direction until the equilibrium is re-established, so, the solubility of substances decreases but Ksp remains same because it is an equilibrium constant which depends only on temperature.

blocks.title: Condition of Precipitation
blocks.text:
Ionic product (IP) of an electrolyte is defined in the same way as Ksp. The only difference is that ionic product (IP) expression contains the initial concentration of ions or the concentration at any time (Solution is under saturated or over saturated) whereas the expression of Ksp contains only saturated condition (equilibrium) concentration.

• IP < Ksp : The solution is unsaturated, and precipitation will not occur.
    • IP = Ksp : The solution is saturated, and solubility equilibrium exists.
    • IP > Ksp : The solution is supersaturated and hence precipitation of the compound will occur.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Treating a non-electrolyte as an electrolyte
Electrolytes are substances that dissociate into ions when dissolved in water, allowing the solution to conduct electricity, sugar (sucrose) is a non-electrolyte

Non-electrolytes, on the other hand, do not dissociate into ions in solution and therefore do not conduct electricity, sodium chloride (NaCl) is an electrolyte.

  • Assuming that weak electrolytes produce the same number of ions as strong electrolytes when, in fact, they produce fewer ions despite having the same concentration as compared to strong electrolyte.
  • Assuming ionization or dissociation happens in the same way in all solvents, neglecting the fact that solvents like water are key to the process.
  • Assuming that the degree of ionization (α) is directly proportional to the concentration of the weak electrolyte, but it is inversely proportional to the square root of it's concentration .

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Using an incorrect value for Kw, such as assuming it is always 1×10−14 regardless of temperature, remember, Kw​ is temperature-dependent (At 25∘C, Kw=1×10−14).
  • Neglecting the contributions of H+ and OH− from water itself in extremely dilute solutions of acids or bases, include H+ orOH−  from water autoprotolysis (1×10−7 M at 25∘C) when the acid/base concentration is very low.
  • Believing that neutral solutions always have a pH of 7, At $25^\circ$C, neutral pH is 7, but at other temperatures $pH_{\text{neutral}} = \frac{1}{2} pK_w$.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Not correctly identifying whether a salt is formed from a strong acid and a strong base, a strong acid and a weak base, a weak acid and a strong base, or a weak acid and a weak base, different types of salts exhibit different behaviors in solution, especially in terms of hydrolysis.
  • Forgetting to account for the concentration of the salt in the solution when calculating the degree of hydrolysis or pH, the degree of hydrolysis depends on both the hydrolysis constant (Kh​) and the concentration of the salt.
  • Not considering the common ion effect in solutions where the salt dissociates into ions that are already present in the solution.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Treating strong acids or bases as weak acids or bases in a buffer system, Strong acids (e.g., HCl) and strong bases (e.g., NaOH) dissociate completely in water and do not form a buffer. Only weak acids or bases, which do not dissociate completely, can form effective buffers.
  • Using the wrong pKa or pKb value for the acid or base, always check that the pKa or pKb values used are correct and applicable to the substances in your buffer system.
  • Miscalculating the ratio of the concentrations of acid and base, ensure that the ratio of the base and acid concentrations is correct in the Henderson equation. If the concentrations are mixed in equal amounts, the ratio should be 1, but if they differ, this should be reflected in the equation.
  • Not accounting for volume changes when adding acid/base to the buffer solution, when add a strong acid or base to a buffer, the volume and concentration of the acid/base components may change. You should consider the dilution effect and recalculate the concentrations if necessary.
  • Using the buffer in a pH range outside its effective range, buffers are effective only within a specific pH range, typically within ±1 pH unit of the pKₐ. Make sure the target pH falls within this range for the buffer to be effective.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Mixing up solubility and solubility product.
  • Applying the concept of Kₛₚ to strong electrolytes like NaCl or KNO₃ while Kₛₚ is only applicable .
  • Assuming that a sparingly soluble salt  dissociates completely in solution when calculating Kₛₚ, some salts, such as AgCl, only partially dissociate in water. Overestimating dissociation can lead to incorrect Kₛₚ values and solubility predictions.
  • Ignoring the effect of common ions in a solution when calculating solubility, the presence of a common ion (an ion already present from another source) will shift the dissolution equilibrium, reducing the solubility of the salt according to Le Chatelier's Principle. This is often ignored in calculations.
  • Using the wrong stoichiometry when writing the Kₛₚ expression.
  • Using Kₛₚ to predict precipitation without calculating the ionic product (Qₛₚ), the precipitation of a salt occurs when the ionic product $Q_{sp}$ exceeds $K_{sp}$. If $Q_{sp}$>$K_{sp}$, precipitation occurs; if $Q_{sp}$ < $K_{sp}$, no precipitation will occur.

blocks.title: Ostwald’s Dilution Law
blocks.text: According to Ostwald’s dilution law when solution of a weak electrolyte is diluted then the degree of ionization of weak electrolyte increases, and at infinite dilution it remains 100% dissociated. ($\alpha \propto \sqrt{\text{Dilution}}$ )
